name: Two Sum
description: Given an array of integers nums and an integer target, return indices of the two numbers such that they add up to target. You may assume that each input would have exactly one solution, and you may not use the same element twice. You can return the answer in any order.
shortDescription: Find two numbers that add up to target

explanation.idea: For each number, the partner you need is fixed: target minus that number. So instead of trying every pair, remember what you've already seen and ask "have I met my partner yet?" in one step.
explanation.analogy: At a party where everyone needs a dance partner of a specific height, you don't measure yourself against every guest. You write each guest's height on a board as they arrive, and check the board for the height you need.

computeWithHashMap.summary: One pass: check the map for the complement before storing the current number.
steps: Create a map from number → its index.
For each index i, compute complement = target − nums[i].
If the complement is already in the map, its stored index and i are the answer.
Otherwise store nums[i] → i and move on. Checking before storing stops a number pairing with itself.
computeWithHashMap.timeWhy: Each number is looked at once, and a hash map lookup or insert is O(1) on average.
computeWithHashMap.spaceWhy: In the worst case every number is stored before the pair is found.

computeWithHashMapTwoPass.summary: Fill the whole map first, then look up each complement.
steps: First loop: store every number → index (a later duplicate overwrites an earlier one).
Second loop: for each i, look up target − nums[i].
Accept it only if the stored index is not i itself, so 3 + 3 = 6 doesn't reuse one 3.
computeWithHashMapTwoPass.timeWhy: Two separate passes over n numbers, each step O(1).
computeWithHashMapTwoPass.spaceWhy: The map holds every distinct number.

computeWithBruteForce.summary: Try every pair i < j until one adds up to target.
steps: For every j after i, check nums[i] + nums[j] == target.
computeWithBruteForce.timeWhy: About n²/2 pairs are checked in the worst case.
computeWithBruteForce.spaceWhy: Only two loop counters are used.

pitfalls: Storing before checking lets an element pair with itself (target 6 with a single 3).
Returning the values instead of the indices.
Sorting first to use two pointers loses the original indices unless you keep them.
interview: Start with brute force in one sentence, then say "I can trade memory for time with a hash map". That shows the reasoning, not memory.
Follow-up: if the array is sorted, two pointers solve it in O(1) extra space (see Two Sum II).
Follow-up: if many targets are queried, build the map once and reuse it.
